newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Austrian press slams government over Iran report.
newsitem.headline: Austrian press slams government over Iran report.

text.p: A government report on Austria's role in the flight of suspected Iranian killers eight years ago raised more questions than it answered and strengthened the case for a parliamentary inquiry, newspapers said on Wednesday.

They echoed opposition condemnation of the 200-page document, which opposition parties have called a smokescreen, and joined calls for a full investigation into events that followed the 1989 murders in Vienna of Iranian Kurdish leader Abdorrahman Qasemlu and two other activists.
The report was presented on Tuesday by Justice Minister Nikolaus Michalek.
"The details of the Iran affair will only come out if all those involved are required to give evidence under oath, as would be the case before a parliamentary committee," the daily Kurier wrote.

Senior diplomats and former Iranian president Abolhassan Bani-Sadr have alleged that Austrian ministers bowed to economic and political pressure from Tehran and colluded in the flight of two of the three suspected Iranian assassins.
Warrants for their arrest were issued only when they were outside the country.

The government report, compiled by the foreign, interior and justice ministries, rejected the claims and the ruling coalition of Social Democrats and conservative People's Party concluded there was no need for an independent inquiry.
"The government has pulled the wool over the government's eyes," wrote the Salzburger Nachrichten daily in a stinging editorial.
"(If the government can investigate itself) then firms may as well audit their own accounts, learner drivers issue their own licences and students mark their own papers," it continued.

Leader writers reserved their strongest criticism for the foreign ministry, then headed by former People's Party leader Alois Mock. His chief aide at the time was Thomas Klestil, the current Austrian president.

The foreign ministry contribution, an unsigned chronology without accompanying documents, contradicted earlier claims by Mock that his department had not passed on Iranian concerns over the case. The foreign ministry had informed other ministries that Iran was pressing Austria to allow the suspects to leave the country, the papers showed.

The report also revealed that former justice minister Egmont Foregger misled parliament in November 1989 when he told deputies there had been no contact between the foreign and justice ministries during the police investigation.
"It is unclear why Foregger, who has an otherwise unblemished record, would commit such a cardinal sin against parliamentary democracy," Kurier wrote.
"This report is not worth the paper it is written on," said Joerg Haider, leader of the far-right Freedom Party. "It is like asking a drunk driver to carry out his own breath test."
The two ruling parties used their parliamentary majority last week to vote down an opposition motion for a parliamentary inquiry.
